reachable: Yes, and unusually cleanly for this axis. The objective runs only inside harness._train, so its influence on the scored prediction is entirely through training gradients — there is no observation-presence gate anywhere in it, so the failure mode that has already been fatal once in this search does not apply. Every stage of the claimed mechanism was verified to fire on real batches: (1) segmentation is exact — 64 rows per batch have prev == 0 and there are exactly 64 sequences per batch, at every step probed, so cumsum yields correct per-trajectory ids; (2) equivalence classes separate cleanly (duplicates at ~4e-6 vs thr_eq ~2e-4); (3) generic marking catches 34.7-38.7% of rows with a top class of 610-649, and gives them listwise weight 0.025 vs 0.71 for ordinary rows; (4) the transported mark fires on 5.1-6.3% of rows every batch across steps 1/100/1000/3000, never empty; (5) transported rows get row weight 6.41 vs 0.71 (9x) and carry 32-42% of the listwise mass and 41-57% of the total per-row gradient norm. The command gate is exactly 0.0 when any qualifying prior carried an identical command (verified numerically), and the min-over-priors correctly implements the "every earlier occurrence carried a different command" wording. The margin hinge and both cross-entropies are formed in dist2 = ((pred - cand)**2).mean(-1), byte-for-byte the decision variable cups_probe._nway uses. Anti-collapse holds: constant prediction 5.084, zero prediction 5.078, exact prediction 0.578. WANTS_CTX is picked up by the harness (verified through G.load_objective). No NaN paths: every logsumexp mask retains at least the diagonal, and the empty-prior/empty-local branches multiply out to zero rather than dividing by it.
solves_outside_model: No — this is the legitimate kind of command use, and I checked it specifically because several r4 candidates parse command text. This module never touches a command STRING: it reads only ctx["cmd"] (the frozen command embedding the model already gets as input), ctx["prev"] (the strict-causal previous observation embedding) and tgt (the label), all inside torch.no_grad(), and it uses them only to compute per-row weights, a candidate mask and a margin. Nothing it derives is ever written into a token, and loss() is called from exactly one place, harness._train — it cannot execute at scoring time. The routing structure it recovers ("this row's target duplicates a non-generic target seen earlier in this trajectory under a different command") is a LABEL-space fact, so it shapes the loss and selects which rows get pressure; the model still has to integrate the move commands to satisfy it. The prior retraction's shape — resolved routing reaching the model as input at the scored read — is structurally impossible for an objective-axis change of this form, and this one does not attempt it. The one honest residual risk, which the author states himself, is that the transport CE can be satisfied by "copy the most recently exposed content", a move-order-position heuristic that does not cancel in the paired difference; the restricted-candidate-set-plus-margin is the intended guard and I could not test whether it is strong enough without training.
summary: The code does what its hypothesis says, and the central mechanistic claim survives the sharpest test I could put to it. I reconstructed the real training path (data/dockerfs3-cupsF-treat-nocwd cache, standardized, split_train_dev seed 0, the genome's own r6 batcher at bs=64, baseline_interleave collate) and mapped every marked row back to its raw train.jsonl step. The transported mark is not an incidental artifact: at step 1, of the 96 rows it marks, 44 are role=cvar_test and 43 are role=cups_test — the read-after-move test steps — plus 6 read and 3 cups_ctx; at step 1000 it is 67 cvar_test + 44 cups_test + 2 read out of 113. Their prior occurrences are the corresponding *_expose steps, i.e. the same content read earlier under its pre-move path (e.g. `cat /tmp/w/cups/opt/app/conf/settings.yaml.2` marked against a prior `cat /tmp/w/cups/g33/f531.bin`). That is precisely the row type the hypothesis claims to select, at ~90-95% precision, and it is what the scored windows measure. Every sample-derived number in the hypothesis reproduces EXACTLY from evolve/jail_data/train_sample.jsonl in pure Python (227 of 724 empty-observation rows, class sizes 35 / 18 / 4, 8.29% transported, 1.66% same-command re-reads), so the author did the work he could do in the jail honestly. The structural claims all hold: segmentation by zero-prev is exact (64 starts, 64 sequences), the equivalence threshold never merges distinct contents, generic pooling means the ~620-strong empty-observation class is a multi-positive rather than 620 mis-directed negatives, the restricted candidate set is own-class ∪ same-trajectory-distinct-non-generic, MSE sits at weight 1.0, and every distance is the eval's own mean-per-dim squared L2. The divergences are all in numbers the author could NOT have measured without torch and stated as measured anyway: the "falling to ~26% once it fits well" self-limiting claim is false under my proxy (it plateaus at 42-47%, because the focal factor floors at ~0.77 since mean nll floors at 1.45 even at pred == tgt exactly), the 39 ms cost is really ~64 ms on this CPU, and the "two to three orders of magnitude" duplicate-vs-distinct separation is really 1.2 to 2.1 orders. None of those change what the mechanism is or where it applies pressure. What I could NOT check: whether comp_ca actually moves (I did not train — no GPU here and the 4000-step budget is out of reach on CPU); the gradient-share trajectory under real training rather than synthetic predictions; whether the depth-3/4 eligible windows contain chains whose contents were exposed earlier under a different path, which is the author's own listed failure mode and is a property of the scored slice, not the training set I measured; GPU-lane timing; and whether the 6x boost costs enough general fit to drag the pick-rate gate down. I modified nothing in the repo, installed nothing, and wrote only to the session scratchpad.

divergences.claim: "Here transported rows carry 55-77% of the gradient norm while the model is still poorly fit, falling to ~26% once it fits well -- the pressure is self-limiting, and full-weight MSE on every row is untouched underneath it, so general prediction is not traded away."
divergences.what_the_code_does: The high end reproduces, the self-limiting part does not. On a real training batch (n=1892, D=768, batcher r6, step 1) the transported rows' share of the per-row gradient norm of the FULL loss is 0.571 at random-init-scale pred, 0.406 at pred=0.5*tgt+0.5*noise, 0.425 at pred=tgt+0.1*noise and 0.467 at pred=tgt+0.02*noise. It plateaus around 42-47%, it never approaches 26%. The structural reason: the only damping device is focal = 1-exp(-nll), but mean nll floors at 1.454 even when pred == tgt EXACTLY (near-duplicate-but-distinct targets remain hard negatives at temp = 0.125*mean_off), so focal floors near 0.77 and never switches the pressure off; and neither the transport CE nor the hinge carries a focal factor at all. Also note the author had no torch, so no gradient-norm share could have been measured.
divergences.evidence: scratchpad/probe4.py and probe7.py on the real standardized cache data/dockerfs3-cupsF-treat-nocwd. probe4: transported share of grad-norm = 0.571 / 0.406 / 0.425 / 0.467 across the four fit levels (transported rows = 5.1% of rows). probe7 term breakdown at pred==tgt exactly: mse 0.0, listwise 0.5306, trans 0.029, hinge 0.0186, mean_nll 1.4538 — identical to the pred=tgt+0.1*noise row, i.e. the contrastive pressure is flat in fit quality.

divergences.claim: "Cost, unmeasured on the real harness: ... Measured at n = 1984, D = 768 on CPU: 39 ms per forward+backward of the loss alone"
divergences.what_the_code_does: This measurement could not have been taken — the inventor jail has no torch. Measured here at n=1892, D=768 on CPU (10 threads): 60.6/61.9/63.9/64.8/67.6 ms, median 63.9 ms; plain MSE fwd+bwd is 2.0 ms on the same tensors. Same order of magnitude as claimed, and still a small fraction of a GPU step, so the cost conclusion stands; the provenance of the number does not, and the BRIEF explicitly asked for performance claims to be stated as unmeasured.
divergences.evidence: scratchpad/probe4.py timing block; PyTorch on this machine, torch.get_num_threads()=10.

divergences.claim: "the closest genuinely distinct pair of observations in this data -- two templated config files differing only in their canary -- sits two to three orders of magnitude above the threshold"
divergences.what_the_code_does: The separation is real and safe but overstated, and the identity of the closest pair is different. Scanning 30 real batches: the smallest distinct-pair distance found is 2.966e-3 against thr_eq 1.986e-4, a ratio of 14.9x (1.17 orders of magnitude), not 100-1000x. Per-batch minima ranged 33x-141x. The closest pair is two dpkg .triggers files differing in a version string (dh_makeshlibs/13.24.1 vs 13.24.2), not two canary-differing config templates. Exact duplicates sit at 3.2e-6 to 4.8e-6, so no merge occurs and the mechanism is not at risk; only the stated margin is inflated.
divergences.evidence: scratchpad/probe8.py: "min distinct-pair distance over sampled batches: 2.9659e-03 (thr 1.986e-04, ratio 14.9)"; probe2.py per-batch: dup max 3.815e-06 / nondup min 2.811e-02 (141.5x), and 6.899e-03 (33-34x) in three other batches.
